utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The initial conversation, sir, well, I didn't do much speaking because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, but that followed that.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Had to do with -- the first meeting with General Gotovina, General Kutil was responding to General Gotovina's actually legitimate complaints that rebel Serbs had entered the zone of separation and which was subsequently proven to be true. On the second one, I believe it had to do with discussions on a Sector South security commission which was a general conversation, and then the subsequents to that had no -- subsequent meeting to that had no relevance to the details of what I've testified to over the previous three days. With regards -- should I proceed to General Cermak, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but perhaps you start to focus on your first meeting with Mr. Cermak which took place in the just of couple of days where you were still there and he had just arrived, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That's when I started --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please tell us the circumstances under which you met him and what the subject of why you are conversation was.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, the first meeting had to do with General Cermak indicating to go us -- he arrived at Sector South headquarters that he was the military governor. He indicated that to the best of my knowledge, he was very keen to work with us and to cooperate with us. He was asking about food and water, did we have enough? Pleasant. Very pleasant, very cooperative. Once again, sir, I, as the Chief of Staff with my commander present, my role was minimal. I did not actually engage with face-to-face discussion with General Cermak until after the activities on the 4th and 5th when I returned some weeks later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, from this occasion, the other occasions where you met him later, did you gain any impression on what actually was within the competence of a -- I think you said military governor of the area, both de facto and as we call it de jure, what were his formal competencies?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand, sir. May I go back to my impressions with General Gotovina and blend the two together or no?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may do so, but we are especially interested -- of course I asked you whether you gained an impression, of course and we are primarily interested in -- on what basis you gained an impression of who said what or if you would pay especially attention to that and whether that would justify the impressions you gained is a separate matter but tell us what impression you gained on the basis of it.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I, as I mentioned, my main role in interacting with General Gotovina was as a supporting element to my commander. My impression of General Gotovina is dynamic, charismatic, aggressive, intelligent, very decisive. And he was -- there was no doubt that he was in charge of the strike force of that zone located in the Sector South region. He was the decisive element whenever we had interactions with subordinate Croatian officers up the 4th and 5th. I, of course, did not see him or interact much at all with him even in a subordinate position with my commander sort of from roughly June onwards. In terms of General Cermak --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will ask you specifically to focus on what you observed and I said what impression you finally gained, whether that's a right one or -- and I invited you specifically to tell us also on the basis of what observations you gained that impression. We have heard about your impressions, we have not heard yet a lot about the details of your observations which led you to gain these impressions.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, vis-a-vis these impressions or opinions of what I formed of General Gotovina, just observing him interact with my area commander, the aura of command that permeated his headquarters, the obvious respect which his subordinate commanders spoke of him and that sort of air of crispness which existed amongst his staff when we arrived and departed. I had one or two meetings with one of his subordinate officers whose name, I believe, was Colonel Kotromanovic that is, I'm not certain of that, who commanded one of General Gotovina's brigades. We met several times and in part, that opinion that I formed of General Gotovina is based on input from Colonel Kotromanovic. Does that answer the questions, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To some extent, yes but I'd like to go into some precision. Would it happen to you, and I'm trying to understand your answer that in your dealings with subordinate officers that they would say, We have to consult General Gotovina. Or would they say, We have to seek instructions for this or we cannot decide these matters. Or in what way did this impression emerge?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, when dealing with the Croatian army elements or the Croatian army liaison officer office, it was enormously rare to get a decision on any issue without it being referred to superior headquarters. I cannot recall, though, General Gotovina's name being mentioned as the specific individual by subordinates to whom they'd have to seek a decision but it was at times quite frustrating for the UN forces to try and get issues resolved at a low level with the Croatian army because almost all decisions involving even minor issues appeared to have to be centralised by the Croatian army liaison officer staff or superior headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that gave you the impression that there was a rather strict hierarchy; is that ...

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now, did it ever happen to you that when you were observing or in any other way learned about any dealings with Mr. Gotovina that he ever said, I have to seek instructions from a higher command or ... if you don't remember tell us, but ...

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I -- if you will just give me a second. There is one issue but I'm just trying to remember if I was there. The issue had to do with movement into the zone of -- up to the zone of separation by the Croatian army in an operation called Lightening and the sector commander was trying to get the Croatian forces to push back and we were told that no such activity was possible without reference from General Gotovina's OP zone to higher and of course that was never granted. But I can't recall if I was there or not. That is the only instance that I can speak of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. I think I stopped you when you wanted to move on to Mr. Cermak. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir. General Cermak was, as I mentioned, arrived, I believe on the 6th at Sector south headquarters and I once again -- he was very conciliatory. He was very concerned. He was very cooperative. He then left after his initial meeting with General Forand and the next time I saw him was a couple of weeks later when a team of us arrived from UNCRO to commence the detailed discussions on how to move the hundreds of Serbian displaced persons from our compound via Croatia into Serbia. To be honest, General Cermak was very cooperative. He -- I think, though I won't pretend to know him well, we got on well. He appeared to be quite frustrated about his inability to make decisions to make life easier for some of the Serbian displaced persons, but he was not disloyal to his chain of command. He was under an enormous amount of pressure always. He always looked as if he had the entire weight of the world on his shoulders. He -- there were occasions when we were trying to get an issue resolved where one of the team that I was with would make a statement and General Cermak would occasionally leave the room to see if the issue could be resolved and then he'd come back and more times than not, it could not be. I had no proof that he was checking with his higher headquarters. That's an assumption on my part. Sir, does that ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said that he expressed frustration in relation to his inability to make decisions. Were there other moments where he showed ability to make decisions to you and then apart from the situation you just described, that he would leave the room. So that in a direct conversation he would say, okay, I'll arrange this or I'll do that or I'll take care of that? I'm trying to get an impression on whether apart from being frustrated and not being able to decide matters whether there were other instances where he showed an ability.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I honestly believe General Cermak was trying to do all that he could to help us with the issue that General Al Rodan had tasked me with, which was to assist UNCRO and Sector South in moving the displaced persons out of the compound. On a variety of minor issues he was able to make decisions. On any of the ones that had any sort of political implications or wider implications, absolutely categorically not, and I could sense his frustration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give an example of these minor issues?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allowing a variety of foodstuffs to be delivered to the Sector South compound, expediting the movement of some of the United Nations Human Rights Action officers, I may have that acronym slightly wrong, to get in and out of Knin. The final details of the very complicate move from Sector South headquarters to Serbia via Sector East, setting up where the stop points were going to be, arranging for medical support to the displaced persons en route, feeding arrangements, he was quite decisive and able to resolve those but that was sort of the level of which I got the sense of which his decision making -- it's not fact, it's opinion -- where his decision-making lay on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you describe and I try to understand as good as I can your testimony that all your dealings with Mr. Cermak were about or were directly related to those in the compound leaving, moving in, but nothing which happened outside the compound and unrelated to the presence of UN and civilians in the compound.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Essentially, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer. My next question would be: Have you any knowledge of which troops on the Croatian side were involved in what happened in the morning of the 4th of August, 1995, and the days following? I don't know whether you have any knowledge about it but if so, please tell us about it.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do. I have personal knowledge in the sense that it was the Puma Brigade which first showed up outside or was amongst the elements that first showed up outside our headquarters on the 5th of August. Secondly, there was a variety of documents published by the Croatian military which showed the rough -- and actually in certain cases quite precise lines of advance by the various units which participated in Operation Storm in Sector South. And I believed I attached a copy of a Croatian document as one of my witness statements --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, not all of your witness statements are in evidence so we cannot rely on anything which is not in evidence. So I haven't seen it during the past few days.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, if you allow me to refer to my notes, that witness statement, I can read it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if that's -- usually witnesses are testifying but if that would refresh your memory and if you say this is an accurate reflection of my observations at that time, then if there is no objection by the parties, I would allow you to read that into the record.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, if you will just give me a sec, I will find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And may I remind you that usually the speed of speech goes up when reading.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir. Sir, from north to south, this Croatian government or Croatian army map indicates the brigades and what routes they took on the assault into the Krajina. And we had the 7th Brigade which was to the north, we had the 134th which was slightly south of that. We had the 134th, the 113th, the 142nd, which was sweeping up from along the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, may I just interrupt one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It might be easier, I believe the General is referring to a map attached to a statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the parties would agree that the witness uses that and that this, then, would be called as a Chamber exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. I just figured it would be easier than ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's -- do we have more copies of it or ... if not then we'll put it on the ELMO and then if ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It might be easier, here is a copy we can put on the ELMO, Judge. It's a little dark. Your Honour, I mean I -- I'm not saying that the map is accurate, it's something that came out of the media. I do believe but I just -- at the risk of just having the General read this through without any reference point, I just figured it was easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Leslie, can you see on your screen at this moment a map which apparently shows troops' movements, is that the ...

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number, sir, I believe indicate brigade-sized elements and the ones in the centre of the screen were what we believed to be those elements under command of General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would there be any troops of this map that would not be under the command of Mr. Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The troops essentially, I believe, sir, my memory is fading, but I believe these elements here were not necessarily under the command of General Gotovina. Oh, I beg your pardon, these elements here were a parallel formation which, if memory serves, were under the command of General Norac but I'd have to go back and check notes, which I do not have readily available. Essentially these elements here and this isn't inclusive or restrictive were under the command of General Gotovina as the operational commander. Subordinate to him were the various brigades which made up his formation including the elements that came up the Livno Valley and through Bosanska Grahovo and down which refers to where I saw what I believe to have been a much more professional anti-tank company from the Serb side pointing towards the Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, may I take it that the Chamber will receive further details of evidence on these matters which will -- yes. Yes, we have -- then just for the record, where the witness initially indicated where the troops were that were not under the command of General Gotovina, he was pointing at the western or southern-western side where he talked about the parallel structure under General Norac, he was referring to the upper part, which I take it to be the northern part, and then when he was referring to those troops that were under General Gotovina's command he was mainly pointing at the centre and the centre east side of this picture. I don't think we have to go into lots of details at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. We at some point and I'm sure that the Prosecution will, will be, of course, giving a detailed map structure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Concerning the formations to the Chamber. I offered this map to the General because this is one that has been published. It's not accurate per se there will be more detail on that accuracy. The General is 100 per cent correct with regards to elements in the north and what was sector north being part of General Norac's units but while we are talking about this and generally those areas under command, we will be presenting a more precise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- map to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber asks these kinds of questions because we get information which is very much isolated and is not in any relation yet to this case to the extent that this is not a case about events but this is a case about whether or not three accused are responsible for certain events. But we'll not at this moment go into further detail in this respect. If you have one second. Yes. I'd like to go back to one of your previous answers. This map, may I take it, is this a spare copy you would like to make available?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Judge, you can have that copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take care that it will be uploaded into the e-court system, and Mr. Tieger, no objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Mr. Registrar, that would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours this becomes Exhibit C1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And C1 is admitted into evidence. In one of your previous answers you referred to issues that had any sort of political implications or wider implications where you said Mr. Cermak could not -- was -- felt frustrated by not being able to make any decisions. Could you give us an example of what kind of issues of political implication or of wider implication?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, one of the principal issues of moving or getting agreement to move the displaced persons from our compound to Serbia had to do with a variety of Serbs who the Croats accused of war crimes. That was a lengthy, politically-charged series of discussions with the eventual resolution being the Human Rights Action Teams from the United Nations supervised the transfer into custody of a number of Serbs from our compounds into a variety of detention facilities run by the Croatian government, and as far as I know that all went well, as well as these things do. There was a whole series of subdiscussions around that central issue, some of which were very mundane and I am trying to think of a specific example, one will come to me shortly, in which General Cermak, it was apparent, had absolutely or very little say in any of its resolution. The support and cooperation to Sector South from the moment I left, I can't really qualify with any expertise or comment on with any expertise because I was gone and I was then essentially an occasional visitor to Sector South as I was to the other sectors in UNCRO. I know that at some point, there was discussions of burning and looting that was happening in the Sector South area. I am very confident I brought them up, but I cannot recall eliciting any response from General Cermak in the sense of he didn't express any -- there was no resolution of that. I think it was more a comment from us to him, but he didn't appear to have any -- well, there was no response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This was during the meetings that you had after you had left.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, when we would return. But it was not a main topic of discussion because such issues were essentially dealt with by Sector South and we were very focused, us from UNCRO, on the movement of the displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you told us on the basis of this published, let's say, sketch, which troops under the command of Mr. Gotovina were involved in the events on the 4th and the 5th. Could you tell us, you told us that you observed troops at the gate of the compound. Could you tell us when these troops -- whether, and if so when these troops left the city of Knin again?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, unfortunately, I cannot, because I had left. I left on the 7th. And the initial troops which showed up at our front gate didn't stay very long and I can deduce why, because they were continuing the advance -- those were the frontline troops continuing the advance in pursuit of the retreating Serbs. Now, I can't tell you who -- what the command and control arrangement for the troops that showed up at the front gate to replace those initial ones, I don't know which unit they came from. In terms of the larger context, the information or intelligent functions at UNCRO headquarters were of the opinion that within about three or four days, most of General Gotovina's frontline professional fighting brigades were essentially clear of what we would call the traditional Sector South boundaries and were continuing the attack or the consolidation. That is the extent of my knowledge. I cannot tell you who had command of what troops at what time based on personal observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So when you are talking about the fighting brigades that apparently had left within three or four days, that under what command the remaining units or forces or soldiers were, you cannot tell us.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. But I have been told subsequent to my departure that General Cermak, as the military governor of Knin, had responsibility for the governor's troops which formations comprised his troops and at what point did General Gotovina have command responsibility over the rear echelons of his fighting brigades which may have been in and around Knin, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you said, "I have been told." Could you tell us by whom.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The intelligence officers at UNCRO headquarters and general discussions amongst a variety of senior officers at both UNPF and UNCRO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This was not detailed information but information of a general nature about command moving without a clear picture; is that ...

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as a word picture, and this is a generalisation. General Gotovina was seen as the war fighter and General Cermak was seen as the administrator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, last question or perhaps last couple of questions. You just mentioned the issue of looting which you raised during one of your later conversations. Did you in any way personally observe any looting or burning, either within the city of Knin or outside the city of the Knin?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. There was a couple of vehicles that had been abandoned by Serbs in close proximity to the headquarters, you could see some Croatian soldiers rummaging through the vehicles. I did not see any looting inside Knin without one very minor exception. And to be fair, to be fair, that one incident I saw, one could argue that that may be someone was searching that vehicle to see if there was any explosives or such but ... However, on subsequent trips into and through the zone, there were numerous instances when I saw smoke plumes on the horizon, occasionally burning buildings, and in close proximity, Croatian soldiers, but I cannot tell you what the units of these Croatian soldiers were. And there's a variety of statements and notes which I and others have provided to the Prosecution which make specific references and dates and times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told us that you cannot tell us what the units of these Croatian soldiers were. Could you give us, apart from what units they belonged, give us an impression? Was the looting done in an organised way? For example, in groups of soldiers, eight or ten, sharing transportation facilities? Or did you get the impression that it was rather individual, one or two? Could you tell us a bit more about what you observed which could assist us in better understanding what -- whether these were individual actions or whether this was part of some structure?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, in my opinion, and of course I did not personally see -- I did not physically see, with the exception of that minor incident outside the compound with the vehicle, I did not physically see Croatian soldiers actually engaged in the act of looting. Nor did I ever personally catch or see a Croatian soldier burning a house. But in broad daylight, sometimes weeks after Operation Storm, we would be driving down a road and there would be a house burning with Croatian soldiers in a substantial group in close proximity to that house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Substantial group for you is ...

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: 30 to 40, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 30 to 40. Croatian soldiers dressed in full uniform?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were -- sir, they were dressed in full uniform but they were not dressed in combat gear. In other words, they had weapons but they were not covered in ammunition, grenades, and all the normal paraphernalia of soldiers expecting imminent combat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This about burning, about looting, did you observe scenes which gave you the impression that they were related to looting? I can imagine that, for example, if you see a soldier driving in a truck with six washing machines at the back, that you could wonder whether he is selling washing machines or whether he was doing something else. I'm just giving this example as I want to -- this Chamber wants to hear the facts you personally observed which you link to looting, if there were any.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I was aware of numerous reports of other people who had seen looting, but I cannot look you in the eye and tell you that I personally saw anything resembling the word picture that you describe. I did not see it myself. There was debris on the side of the roads, there was, you know, sheets and beddings over windows, but I did not see a Croatian soldier carrying a trophy of some kind down the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has no further questions for you. If the questions by the Chamber has triggered any need by the parties to put additional questions, a limited opportunity will be given. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If we could just take a quick break to consult with co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please take your time. Meanwhile, I'll ask you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I didn't, Your Honour, I, in discussions with my learned friend, I am going to turn the floor over to Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, these questions arise from the questions by the Bench and if you can understand that as well, Mr. Leslie. I'm asking you questions now on behalf of Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The first matter I want to deal with is the issue of Mr. Cermak helping you in relation to the displaced persons. These questions haven't come about in the prepared form because they come from the Bench so I've had no notice of them but I have, in the back of my mind, that a letter was written complimenting Mr. Cermak. Did you write a letter? I know General Forand did.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I cannot recall, and I would -- I would doubt if I would write the letter because General Al Rodan that would be his remit, he as the responsible commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And I'm not putting it as a fact as I am remembering 5.000 documents in my head as I ask this question, and it wasn't expected by me. I just had a feeling that you wrote the letter but you certainly can't remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I doubt if I would have written -- at that time, I didn't work for General Forand, I worked for General Al Rodan so I would have not written General Forand's draft. I cannot recall writing such a letter for my commander, General Al Rodan and I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Fine. The issue or not of the letter is irrelevant, in a way. It was actually the support of General Cermak in relation to this particular issue of the movement of the people from Knin and transferring them to Bosnia or Serbia by which you were impressed in relation to the steps he'd taken.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, sir, without meaning to distract the Court at all, I remember General Cermak and I talking that when this was all over, we would commiserate and have a beer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to turn now to a matter of slight substance in your evidence to the Bench, and that's this issue of calling him the military governor. Now, presumably, you talked to General Cermak through an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did that interpreter always be the same interpreter or did the interpreter change?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not bring my own interpreter. I cannot recall, but I think it is a safe assumption for me to say that more often than not, it would probably be the same person provided by Sector South headquarters, but I cannot attest to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Because you weren't a B/C/S speaker, as we call it in these courts.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And you gave the date of the 6th of August when Mr. Cermak visited the UNCRO camp. We actually have evidence in the court that establish it was the 7th of August when Mr. Akashi visited.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that was the day you departed Knin as well?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I left just after Mr. Akashi and General Forand had a discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. And were you there when General Cermak had any discussions with General Forand or Mr. Akashi?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there when General Cermak first arrived and greeted him, brought him into the operations centre. They, being General Forand, Mr. Akashi and General Cermak, I believe, then went up to General Forand's office and I was not included in that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But this was -- were you there when Mr. Akashi toured the camp, met the people, spoke to people on the ground?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah. And that was part of a fairly substantial delegation of people?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah. I was putting it conservatively, but there was a lot of interest in this visit from Mr. Akashi?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. The issue of the military governor as a title. You would be aware of it being a title of significance, perhaps, in relation to NATO forces or western forces as a particular position within occupied territories; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On this occasion, of course, the area we're dealing with wasn't, in fact, occupied territory by the Croatian forces, it was indeed part of Croatia itself.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The internationally-recognised boundaries of Croatia included the terrain formerly occupied by the ARSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. These forces from the Croatian army were not upon foreign soil as sometimes happen in the experience of your armed forces, the armed forces of many people in this room, when they, so to speak, get into a position of occupation on foreign soil.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you're asking me a question which has a variety of legal strands with which I'm not familiar. I think I'm outside my sandbox now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any dispute about this between the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why ask the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's because it helps in development of the next question and it's unsettling if I don't lead it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The parties don't have a dispute about the positive -- yes, they were not on foreign soil.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely, sir. It just shows that I'm trainable. So, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But the issue being that were you aware that in fact within the Croatian legal system, system of government, there is no such position as military governor?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you, in fact, aware of the actual position that Mr. Cermak was appointed as holding when he arrived in Knin on the 6th of August and kept for the duration of his stay there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just for clarification, I take it that Mr. Kay is seeking to elicit whatever information the witness might have about the formal position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that that's what you're seeking at this moment, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, could we cover that in one rather general question because if the witness has no knowledge about the formal position of what -- the position, in formal terms, the position in which Mr. Cermak was appointed, then we can leave it aside. The Chamber of course has received meanwhile some evidence on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And we're not going through that again, but I don't know whether the witness knows or not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but if we just put one general question. Were you in any way familiar with the precise position in which Mr. Cermak was appointed at that time and what competences, what powers that decision would give, how it was structured in the state organisation of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You weren't aware that he had the position of "zborno mjeste" of Knin, the garrison commander of Knin?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you look at letters from Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure I saw letters that Mr. Cermak may have or General Cermak may have exchanged with General Forand, but I can't recall with any degree of precision the content or the signature block.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you ever note that within those letters, there was no title of military governor, but in fact, ZM Knin?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. It seems, from what you are saying, that someone told you that he was the military governor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm -- that was, I believe, the standard appelation with which most Sector South personnel described General Cermak, but I can't tell you where that name came from or that title came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And I don't disagree with that, General, you're not on your own here and that's an issue in the case. But the title of military governor was not something from, as I understand it -- your evidence to be, that you actually investigated yourself?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And wherever military governor came from, you would agree, would you not, that if it was wrong, then that is something that has incorrectly been passed down the chain?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, all the answers that the witness has given on your questions are answers that almost logically follow from the answer to the question I put to him and unless there's any specific issue you'd like to deal with, the Chamber got your point that the awareness of the formalities of the position of Mr. Cermak were at a rather low level with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Again, I have to ask this as a prelude to the next question, I hope the Bench are understanding about that. You've already said that the tasks and responsibilities of Mr. Cermak were not known by you in any sort of detail?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You only knew, I presume, what he did from what he did.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you never saw him commanding any troops in the Knin area.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, sir, on the -- the night before the displaced Serbs were to leave our compound, they had fired a large volume of small arms fire over the compound in a show of intimidation and General Cermak arrived and put a very abrupt stop to that, and to me that demonstrates command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How did that happen? Where did the volley of fire come from?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The volley of fire was from Croatian personnel stationed outside the camp it did didn't harm anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It cause the obviously no casualties and we believe it was a means of encouraging those who were about to leave to really make sure that they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the particular individuals firing in that way were whom, how were they identifiable?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, they were not identifiable. I don't believe -- I certainly did not see them fire, I certainly heard it. I was there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: And -- but I did not see -- it only lasted a minute or two and I was gone the next morning. So -- but there was many other people from Sector South who can give you much more detail on this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So we don't know if they were civilians or military personnel?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did you see what Mr. Cermak actually did to stop this?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Suffice it to say, then, from your knowledge and experience of the matter, that something very unpleasant was happening that he put a stop to.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So putting that example then to one side, your dealings with Mr. Cermak come about from matters concerning the UN and the government of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would you like me to sort of just expand it for you --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I think I understand the general context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You understand what I'm putting to you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Just to make it clear, the displaced persons within the camp were a large problem that the UN had for several weeks that needed to be resolved.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was definitely an issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your view then about him having command over troops in the area at some stage who was in that area, is, in fact, based upon information that you've received from others within the UN system.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you would accept, would you not, that that information can be right or wrong?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay. If the witness would say I cannot accept that information that reached me was right or wrong, information is always right or wrong, and there will be a need really any specific situation where someone would be for the full 100 per cent sure that the information is right or is wrong and that is so exceptional that the question -- putting to the question to the witness is -- qualifies more or less a superfluous question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, but the issue itself is large within the case which is why it's of concern arising this way through the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kay, whoever tells this Court that he got information, this Court will always be aware that this information may be right, may be wrong, and we'll consider it always in the context of the totality of the evidence we receive. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm very grateful for that indication from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It comes to it and I can't really develop this issue with you any further, can I, because the -- given the basis of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I am not -- I'm not an expert on General Cermak's Croatian command and control architecture or his terms of reference, so I would agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm very obliged. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that the discussions among Defence counsel and the outcome of that means that there are no further questions by other Defence counsel or is that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour, nothing from General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Leslie, this, then, concludes your testimony in this court we'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for answering all the questions that were put to you, and I usually say I wish you a safe trip home again but in view of your profession, I don't know whether your trip will be home or not. But at least a safe trip wherever you go. Mr. Usher, would you please escort Mr. Leslie out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. It's been an honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to deliver a decision, then have a break, then invite the Prosecution to call its next witness. This is the Chamber's decision on matters relating to the Prosecution's motion requesting the admission of Rule 92 ter statements of Mikhail Ermolaev and Kari Anttila and associated exhibits. The Prosecution filed this motion on the 1st of February 2008. On the 13th of February, 2008, the Cermak Defence filed a response requesting that the Chamber deny the Prosecution leave to conduct an examination in chief to supplement the Rule 92 ter statements, or order the Prosecution to supplement and clarify the statements in written form and in advance of the court hearing. On the 19th of February, 2008, the Prosecution filed a request for leaving to reply and a reply. On the 27th of February, 2008, the Chamber decided to grant the Prosecution's request for leave to reply and informed the parties accordingly, through an informal communication. The Gotovina and Markac Defence did not file any responses on this matter, and the time to do so has run out. None of the Defence teams objected to the admission of the Rule 92 ter statements and the associated exhibits. The Chamber will deal with this matter at the appropriate time during the testimony of the two witnesses in question. As for the Cermak Defence's requests, this Chamber follows the practice of many other Chambers at the Tribunal in allowing the Prosecution to conduct an examination in chief to supplement the Rule 92 ter statement of a witness. The Chamber expects the Prosecution to clarify -- to clarify as necessary portions of the statement, without eliciting the same evidence viva voce. As an exception, the Chamber expresses a strong preference for receiving in the form of viva voce testimony, important evidence that goes to acts and conduct of the accused. As for the Cermak Defence's concerns regarding adequate notice of the evidence that the Prosecution intends to lead, this is a matter to be addressed through proper disclosure by the Prosecution. The requests of the Cermak Defence are therefore denied in their entirety. This concludes the Chamber's decision. We'll now have a break. We'll resume at 20 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honours, Ruth Frolich. The Prosecution calls Mile Sovilj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No protective measures, Ms. Frolich.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Mr. Usher, would you please ... Perhaps I could already inquire with the Defence whether the new statement and the new exhibits cause any problems which would amount to objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since the witness has now entered the courtroom, Mr. Mikulicic. Yes, the witness -- good afternoon, Mr. Sovilj. I take. Mr. Sovilj, before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, the nothing but the truth. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration of which the text is now handed out to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, I solemnly swear that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sovilj. Please be seated. Ms. Frolich.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sovilj, or should I say good afternoon. Could you please state your full name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Mile Sovilj.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Did you give a statement to the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor on the 22nd of February, 2007?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a problem. My translation is in French now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Channel 4 is English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah, I receive English on channel 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It must be just me then, Your Honour, because ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's test it again whether your channel 4 is -- please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. President, would it be helpful if the usher could provide the witness with a B/C/S version of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that's very practical.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Could also the 65 ter number 04834 be presented on the screen and marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. Sovilj, on the screen in front of you, you also have, you I believe you can see the statement. Is this the statement that you gave to the representatives of the OTP on the 22nd of February, 2007?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Now, after your statement was recorded, was it read back to you in the language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Sorry, could we just flip through the pages of the statement, go to page 2, and page 3, and page 4. And finally, page 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sovilj, did you sign the English version of the statement?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any use to have on our split screen two English versions rather than on the one side --

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Oh, I apologise, Mr. President, I didn't notice that both were in English. No, I believe that B/C/S version would be on one side of the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, as it was in the beginning. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Is this your signature that you see on the screen? Sorry, not on this page of the interpreter's certification, I'm sorry, if we could go back one page in both versions, please?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to review the statement in a language you understand yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: And did you make some corrections to that statement?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Could 65 ter 04854 be shown on screen, please and marked for identification. Now, Mr. President, we still do not have the B/C/S translation of this statement, it was taken yesterday so we only have the English copy to work with.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. Sovilj, is this -- are these -- is this the statement containing the corrections that you made yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: This thing now is in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. Sovilj, did you sign -- were the corrections that you made yesterday read back to you in the language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: And did you sign the English version of that statement?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. Sovilj, is this your signature on the bottom left corner?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: If you flip to the second page.

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Is this your signature at the bottom of -- at the bottom left corner of this page?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: If we go one more page. Is this your signature at the bottom left corner?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: And one more page, please. Is this your signature at the bottom, left corner?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: And the last page, please. Is this your signature, Mr. Sovilj?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, these two statements that are read together are they -- do they accurately reflect what you said to the representatives of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: And these two statements taken together, are they in full accordance with the truth to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: If you were asked the same questions today, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, with your leave, we would like to tender both statements into evidence under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections against the admission of these 92 ter statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No objections from the Gotovina Defence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Mr. Registrar, the first statement is the 22nd of February, 2007 statement. That would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P86, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P86 is admitted into evidence. And the other one is the statement of I think it was yesterday, 23rd of April, 2008, that would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P87, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P87 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Ms. Frolich.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you, with your leave, I would like to read the witness summary now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness is aware of why this is read.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you. Mile Sovilj was born in the village of Kijani in the municipality of Gracac. He lived in the town of Gracac in 1995 and was present when the shelling attack on Gracac started on the 4th of August, 1995. Mr. Sovilj's evidence relates to the circumstances in which he witnessed the shelling of Gracac and left the town and afterwards Croatia after the shelling started. He also relates evidence about the flight of the civilian population from Gracac and his native village of Kijani and about the 14 individuals from Kijani including his father who stayed there and were killed. Finally, Mr. Sovilj relates the information regarding the events preceding Operation Storm that occurred in the Medak pocket in 1993 as well as the circumstances that stopped him from returning to Croatia after he left it on the 5th of August, 1995. That concludes the witness summary, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Frolich.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: I would now like to ask some additional questions of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. Sovilj, how big was the town of Gracac in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: In terms of the population, around 5.000.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: And do you know what was roughly its ethnic composition?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: If we are talking about Gracac itself, Gracac proper, the population was 25 Serb and 75 per cent Croat and other non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm referring to the period in 1995 just before the attack, the shelling attack of the 4th of August, if I did not make myself clear.

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Yes, you could say it was on the eve of Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. Sovilj, if I could refer you to -- I'm sorry, can I -- just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. Sovilj, was there, in fact -- what was the ethnic majority living in the town of Gracac on the eve of the shelling attack on the 4th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Serbian orthodox.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Christian orthodox, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: So in fact when you say that 75 per cent were Croat, did you perhaps mean that 70 [sic] per cent of the population was Serb?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: I don't know what I said that when I was talking about percentages of the population, I meant to say that about 95 per cent were Serbs and five per cent were Croats and other ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Now, Mr. Sovilj, what kind of military training, if any, do you have?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: I did my military service in the former Yugoslav People's Army and after that, I was engaged in military drills several times.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Was this your only military experience?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: If we could have P86 back on the screen just for ease of reference.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. Sovilj, I would like to turn your attention to the events that you describe in paragraph 5 of your statement which is page 2 in both English and B/C/S. Could you tell the Court where were you at around 5.00 a.m. on the 4th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: On the 4th of August, 1995, in the morning, I was in my apartment in Gracac. I lived on Czar Dusan Street as it was called then, 133.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Can you describe what happened at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Around 5.00 a.m., as I was preparing to go on the road, I was about to travel, I heard the explosion of a shell that had fallen at a distance of about 120 metres from my flat.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: How do you know that you heard the explosion of a shell?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: We who lived -- who had lived for several years in the state of war, were able, by then, to distinguish between the sound of a bullet and the sound of another round from the sound of a projectile from a cannon. We could distinguish it by the sound it made as it flew through the air and also the explosion. I want to add that Gracac had already been shelled in 1993 during the Medak Pocket operation and Maslenica operation, so we had some experience.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: How were you able to estimate that the distance was -- of the explosion was about 120 metres from your flat?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Well, a crater was found later in that place with fragments scattered around, debris, branches from a nearby tree.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Can you explain by -- what you mean by that a crater was found? Did you observe this crater yourself? Or did you hear it from someone else?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: I saw it myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: When did you see this crater?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: I can't tell you the hour, but I saw it as I left my apartment to go towards the municipal assembly building in Gracac, it could have been around 9.00 or 10.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: As you left your apartment in Gracac, did you observe any other -- you said you heard shelling, but did you observe any other damage such as you described?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Well, I heard the shelling occasionally, sporadically, I can't tell you in which intervals. Gracac is a population centre that is in terms of configuration and area it covers, rather large. It stretches along -- around 4 kilometres, perhaps a little less, or a little more. In various sections of the town, explosions were heard occasionally that I suppose were from shells and as I was going towards the municipal assembly building, crossing the bridge next to Gradina hill, I saw broken branches of a tree and it all looked like another shell had fallen there as well, but I didn't go closer to see exactly where it happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Could you tell the Chamber where the municipal assembly building is located in Gracac?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: How shall I explain? It's in the centre of the town, the centre of Gracac next to the primary school, next to the former municipal committee building. On the main street.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be sufficient. Can you tell what the frequency of shelling was as you recall it?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Well, all of that was a long time ago, but shells hit occasionally. I can't tell you in what intervals, maybe an hour, maybe half an hour, depending on which period we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: You also say in paragraph 7 of your statement which is I believe is the same page, page 2 of the English version and page 3 of the B/C/S version that you left Gracac around 4.00 p.m. on the same day, on the 4th of August, 1995. Could you tell the Court for how long did the shelling continue during that time, during that period?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Well, as I told you. As I was leaving Gracac, it was around 4.00 p.m. there was sporadic shelling on Gracac town. Later as I was going towards Kijani village, I heard explosions from that direction but whether it was there or somewhere farther away, I could not judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Frolich, the Chamber would say copied, at least the Chamber staff was copied on some e-mail exchanges which would cause us to expect that, apart from hearing from this witness that the municipal council building was next to the school, I don't know where the school is as a matter of fact, so I still do not know where the centre of the town, that there would be maps annotated et cetera. Is that not --

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: I was just about to ask for the map of Gracac, 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because if all the markings are there, we can go there more quickly, it gives us a better impression of just knowing that the building is next to a school building.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Judge. 65 ter 4850 if you can bring it up on screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. Sovilj, do you see the map on screen before you?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: What is this map?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Well, that's a map of Gracac with the surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: And what are these markings?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: A is the location of my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Sovilj, can I just stop you for a moment. Do you recognise these markings as -- I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Who made these markings?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: When did you make them?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Whose signature is this on the bottom left corner of the map?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: It's mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you tell us what marking A represents?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: I said already A is the location of my apartment where I used to live.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: What is marking B?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: B is the place where the first shell I heard fell.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Marking C?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: C is the place near the rivulet otuca near the bridge where I saw the tree with broken branches and where I thought a shell had fallen.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Can you tell us what marking D represents?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: D is the location where the municipal assembly was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Now, without -- would the Chamber be assisted if the witness may perhaps mark also the location of the school or just point to where the school roughly was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm -- the school, until now, played just a role as being adjacent to where the municipal centre building was. That is the only role until now which the school played so therefore there's no need to mark it unless there's anything else you would like to ...

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No, I was merely checking with the Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: What does marking E represent, Mr. Sovilj?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: That is the location of the police station in Gracac.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Marking F?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: That's the railway station.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Marking G?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: G is a hamlet called Surle near Kijani village where my parents used to live before the Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: And finally, marking H?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: H is the road I used to go from Gracac to Surle hamlet on the 4th of August, 1995 after 4.00 p.m. when I left Gracac.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Is marking B the location where you saw the crater of the first impact?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, if this document could be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then no one else jumps up so no objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P88, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P88 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Could we just keep this map on the screen for a little longer.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. Sovilj, did you observe any other damage in Gracac as you walked to the municipal centre?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. Sovilj, do you know what, if any, military facilities there are in Gracac?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: No. In Gracac, there had never been any military installations, barracks, or anything else except, as far as I remember in the beginning of the war in 1991, there used to be some military units and some military equipment, only at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Were there civilians or soldiers or both in Gracac at the time the shelling attack commenced?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Well, in Gracac at the time of the shelling, that is, at the beginning of Operation Storm, civilians were mainly there and as far as I know, there was some people in the police station who constituted the duty service. And 7, 10, 15 days prior to that, everyone of military age capable of carrying a rifle had been mobilised and everyone was on the frontline.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Just to clarify, when you say, "7, 10, 15 days prior to that," you mean -- do you mean Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Just before Operation Storm started, some 10, 15 days earlier and memories are fading, you have to understand, that but generally speaking, everyone capable of carrying a rifle was mobilised and sent to the frontline so only the civilian population remained, women, children, and certain individuals who stayed on duty at the police station, at the assembly building, people who were there on duty so that life could continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: How did the civilian population of Gracac react to the shelling?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: In the course of at that day before 4.00 p.m. when I left Gracac, on two or three occasions, I went to the municipality building and back and you could hardly see anybody on the streets. People were mostly locked up in their apartments, flats, or even shelters that were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: And later on in the afternoon, was the situation the same or different?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: In the course of the afternoon, I noticed the first people who started leaving Gracac and on my return from the municipal building around 2.00 in the afternoon or half past 2.00, I even saw a few tractors fully loaded with their necessities and I could also observe people who started moving from Gracac in the direction of north to Deringaj and Mazba [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, these locations are -- were they in -- with respect to Gracac, the villages ...

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: It is north from Gracac but you can't see it on this map because this map stops right before the village of Deringaj. So you won't see it on this map.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Can you describe the appearance of people who were leaving from Gracac?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Concerned, worried, with an expression on their faces showing pessimism, not very optimistic expression on their faces.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Why did you leave Gracac?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Well, obviously as everybody else, I was afraid so I'd say that I left for safety reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Did you plan to return or not to Gracac at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: I believe that all these people who were leaving Gracac at the time thought that it was only temporary and that they would return sooner or later. However, it turned out that they did not return, only some did a few years later, they returned to go and live there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: You personally, did you have plans for return?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: To be very honest, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Let me turn to another topic now. In paragraph 10 of your statement which is page 3 in both English and B/C/S, you refer to your father. Could you tell us where your -- where did your father live before the 4th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Including the 4th of August and the 5th of August, he lived in the village of Kijani, in the hamlet called Surle.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: And under what circumstances did you first start believing your father was dead?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Immediately after the operation, after Operation Storm and after we fled to Serbia, we tried to get him out of the village but he refused to leave the village. I personally told him that his safety might be at risk but he did not want to leave, even temporarily, but he stayed down there. So when we arrived there, I said some 10 or 15 days later when he didn't turn up that we should report him as missing to the International Red Cross, the Red Cross of Serbia, the then-Yugoslavia, and I did that. I reported his disappearance to UNPROFOR which was still in Krajina, that part of Croatia, that is, and to the Croatian-Helsinki watch. My friend the late Pero Mrkoj [phoen], who was the director of the Helsinki board at the time went and inspected the area and went to Gracac and tried to learn something about my father after I had spoken to him, and he came back to me to tell me that nobody told him anything about my father. His trail was lost. After that, I reported all that to the information and documentation centre Veritas in Belgrade, an institution that also dealt with the issue. In other words, I spoke to all the institutions that might have helped to learn something, but I couldn't learn anything. The information that I received was controversial, mostly wrong, and some year later when I had already lost a hope that I would ever see him alive, I started actually believing that he had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: When did you first learn some concrete information about your father's whereabouts?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: The first concrete piece of information came in 2004 after the exhumation of victims from the Gracac cemetery. I got a call to come to give blood in Zagreb for the -- for DNA analysis.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Was there anything else that happened prior to that identification?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Before that identification, I got a call from the Veritas office in Belgrade. I believe it was in 2002 when that happened. They had received certain photos of bodies which had been found in the area of Gracac and other locations through the exchange with the Croatian side. I went there to possibly recognise my father's body among those photos.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Could we show Exhibit 65 ter 04847, sorry, 65 ter number, not exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. Sovilj, what did you observe when you went to Veritas? What was on the photos of bodies?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: There were a lot of photos depicting bodies. My attention was attracted by a photo of a body which appeared to be a gruesome image. It was a decomposing body that had previously been burned, I believe. I was attracted by one thing in that photo and that was a metal tobacco box, which I had bought my father maybe two years prior to Operation Storm and that my father used to carry on him at all times so at that point, I assumed, I suspected that that might have been my father's body next to that tobacco box.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. Sovilj, do you see the document on the screen in front of you on the right-hand side is the document in the B/C/S version. Now do you recognise what is this document?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Yes, this document is a report on death that I received from the Department of Forensic Medicine in Zagreb when I received the mortal remains of my father at the border crossing between Ilok and Backa Palanka. And before that, the DNA analysis had established a positive identity of my father as one of the bodies that were exhumed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Excuse me, could we scroll back to the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Are there any mistakes in this death certificate that you think should be just corrected for the record?

utterances.speaker: MILE SOVILJ
utterances.text: Just the year of birth, it says 1930 whereas my father was born in 1931. I don't know how this error occurred.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Could this document be tendered into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No one apparently --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
